title: Travel and the verbs of motion
objectives: I can choose between a verb of one direction, such as 'іти́', and the general verb that pairs with it, such as 'ходи́ти', for walking, traveling by vehicle, flying, running and carrying.
I can say where I am going now, where I go regularly, and where I went and came back from.
I can say that someone has set off or will set off with 'піти́' and 'пої́хати'.
I can buy a train ticket, ask about the timetable and say how I travel: by train, by plane, by bus or by taxi.
I can explain the consonant changes in 'ходжу́', 'ї́жджу', 'ношу́', 'вожу́' and 'лечу́', and why the past of 'нести́' is 'ніс'.

vocabulary.source: to go on foot, in general or there and back
vocabulary.note: 'Ходжу́', 'хо́диш', 'хо́дять'. It pairs with 'іти́', the verb of one direction; the two are not an aspect pair. It also means to walk, as an ability.

example.source: Olena walks to work every day.

vocabulary.source: to go by vehicle, in general or there and back
vocabulary.note: 'Ї́жджу', 'ї́здиш', 'ї́здять'. It pairs with 'ї́хати', the verb of one direction, and is used for any vehicle.

example.source: We often go to see Grandma.

vocabulary.note: 'Лечу́', 'лети́ш', 'летя́ть', with the stress on the ending in every form. It pairs with 'літа́ти', the general verb.

example.source: I'm flying to Canada tomorrow.
Taras often flies to Lviv.

vocabulary.source: to carry, on foot, in one direction
vocabulary.note: 'Несу́', 'несе́ш', 'несу́ть'; past 'ніс', 'несла́', 'несли́'. It pairs with 'носи́ти'. The past 'ніс' is spelled like the noun 'ніс', nose.

example.source: What are you carrying?

vocabulary.source: to carry, in general; to wear
vocabulary.note: 'Ношу́', 'но́сиш', 'но́сять'. It pairs with 'нести́'. Clothes that someone wears regularly are carried on the body, so 'носи́ти' also means to wear.

example.source: Oksana often wears a red jacket.

vocabulary.source: to transport, to drive someone, in one direction
vocabulary.note: 'Везу́', 'везе́ш', 'везу́ть'; past 'віз', 'везла́', 'везли́'. It pairs with 'вози́ти'. The person or thing carried is in the accusative.

example.source: The taxi is taking us to the station.

vocabulary.source: to transport, to drive someone, in general

example.target: Цей авто́бус во́зить люде́й до аеропо́рту.
example.source: This bus takes people to the airport.
example.source_literal: This bus transports people to airport.

example.source: I'm running for the train!

vocabulary.note: Like 'чита́ти': 'бі́гаю', 'бі́гаєш'. It pairs with 'бі́гти', and it also means to go running, as a sport.

example.source: Taras goes running in the park in the morning.

vocabulary.source: to go, to set off on foot
vocabulary.note: 'Піду́', 'пі́деш', 'пі́дуть'; past 'пішо́в', 'пішла́', 'пішли́'. The perfective of 'іти́' for setting off. In the past it says that the person has left.

example.source: Taras has already left.

vocabulary.source: to go, to set off by vehicle
vocabulary.note: 'Пої́ду', 'пої́деш', 'пої́дуть'; past 'пої́хав', 'пої́хала', 'пої́хали'. The perfective of 'ї́хати' for setting off.

example.target: У субо́ту ми пої́демо до Льво́ва.
example.source: On Saturday we'll go to Lviv.
example.source_literal: In Saturday we will-go to Lviv.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'по́їзда'; plural 'поїзди́', 'поїзді́в', with the stress moving to the ending.

example.target: Наш по́їзд уже́ стої́ть на вокза́лі.
example.source: Our train is already at the station.
example.source_literal: Our train already stands at station.

example.source: My plane is at nine in the morning.
How do I get to the airport?
My suitcase is very big.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'ро́зкладу'. 'Ро́зклад поїзді́в' is a train timetable, literally 'timetable of-trains'.

example.source: I have the bus timetable.
There are a lot of people in the car.

vocabulary.note: Plural 'місця́', with the stress moving to the ending.

example.source: Is this your seat?
Here is our taxi!

grammar.title: Two verbs for one movement: one direction and in general
grammar.explanation:
English has one verb for each way of moving: 'go', 'fly', 'run', 'carry'. Ukrainian has two verbs for each, and both are imperfective. The first, called here the verb of one direction, presents a movement toward one goal as it happens: 'Я йду в парк.' (I'm walking to the park). The second, the general verb, presents movement that does not have one direction and one goal at this moment: a repeated trip, a trip there and back, movement in many directions, or the ability to move: 'Я ча́сто ходжу́ в парк.' (I often go to the park).

The two verbs are not an aspect pair. Aspect sets a process against one completed whole, and here both verbs present a process. They differ in the shape of the movement: one line toward a goal, or lines in several directions, or a line out and back.

Six pairs are common. The first verb of each pair is the verb of one direction:

- 'іти́' and 'ходи́ти': to go on foot
- 'ї́хати' and 'ї́здити': to go by vehicle
- 'леті́ти' and 'літа́ти': to fly
- 'бі́гти' and 'бі́гати': to run
- 'нести́' and 'носи́ти': to carry while walking
- 'везти́' and 'вози́ти': to carry in a vehicle, to drive someone

Ukrainian also chooses the verb by the way a person travels. 'Іти́' and 'ходи́ти' are for walking; 'ї́хати' and 'ї́здити' are for any vehicle: a car, a bus, a train or a taxi. English 'go' covers both, so 'I'm going to Lviv' is 'Я ї́ду до Льво́ва.', because nobody walks from Kyiv to Lviv. In the same way 'нести́' is to carry something in your hands as you walk, and 'везти́' is to carry it in a vehicle: of a taxi driver taking you to the station, Ukrainian says 'Він везе́ вас на вокза́л.'

A train or a bus that runs on a route can take 'іти́' as well as 'ї́хати': 'По́їзд іде́ до Оде́си.' and 'По́їзд ї́де до Оде́си.' both mean that the train goes to Odesa.

rows: I often go to the park.
The plane is flying to Odesa.
Sam is running for the bus.
The children are running around in the park.
The taxi is taking Oksana to the airport.
The father drives the children to school.

examples.source: I'm walking to the post office.

The train goes to Odesa.
I'm carrying the coffee.

grammar.title: Choosing the verb: one direction or in general
grammar.explanation:
The rule is simple to state. Use the verb of one direction when the movement has one goal and is seen while it happens. Use the general verb for every other movement.

The verb of one direction is used for:

- a movement happening now: 'Я за́раз ї́ду на робо́ту.' (I'm on my way to work now)
- a movement in the past seen while it was happening, often as the background of another event: 'Коли́ я йшов на робо́ту, я зустрі́в Окса́ну.' (When I was walking to work, I met Oksana)
- one trip planned for a set time, in the present tense, as English also does: 'За́втра я лечу́ до Оде́си.' (I'm flying to Odesa tomorrow)

The general verb is used for:

- a habit or a repeated trip: 'Я ча́сто ї́жджу до Льво́ва.' (I often go to Lviv)
- a trip there and back in the past: 'Учо́ра я ходи́в у кіно́.' (Yesterday I went to the movies)
- movement with no single direction: 'Ді́ти бі́гають на ву́лиці.' (The children are running around outside)
- the ability to move, or the activity itself: 'Дити́на вже хо́дить.' (The child can already walk); 'Я люблю́ бі́гати.' (I love running)

The past of a trip there and back needs care, because English says 'went' for both meanings. 'Учо́ра я ходи́в у кіно́.' says that I went to the movies and came back, so it means the same as 'Учо́ра я був у кіно́.', the way the unit on the past said it. The general verb is right even when the trip happened only once: 'Мину́лого лі́та я ї́здила до Оде́си.' (Last summer I went to Odesa). 'Учо́ра я йшов у кіно́.' says only that I was on my way, and it usually leads to what happened on the way.

Some words and phrases point to one verb or the other. These go with the general verb, because they name a repeated or a typical trip:

- 'ча́сто', often
- 'завжди́', always
- 'щодня́', every day
- 'і́ноді', sometimes
- 'ніко́ли', never
- 'ко́жного ти́жня', every week, the genitive of time, like 'мину́лого ти́жня'

'За́раз', now, goes with the verb of one direction, because it places the movement at this moment: 'Куди́ ти за́раз ї́деш?' (Where are you going now?)

Коли́ ми ї́хали до Льво́ва, йшов дощ.
when we went to Lviv, went rain
It was raining while we were traveling to Lviv.
Taras walks to work every day.
Мину́лого ти́жня ми ї́здили до Льво́ва.
of-last of-week we went to Lviv

examples.source_literal: She never not went to Lviv.

examples.source: When I was walking to work, I met Oksana.

grammar.title: The forms: present and past
grammar.explanation:
The general verbs in '-ити' and the verb 'леті́ти' are second conjugation, like 'говори́ти'. Their 'я' form changes the last consonant of the stem, as 'сиді́ти', 'сиджу́' does, and every other form keeps the plain consonant:

- 'ходи́ти': 'ходжу́', 'хо́диш', 'хо́дять'
- 'ї́здити': 'ї́жджу', 'ї́здиш', 'ї́здять'
- 'носи́ти': 'ношу́', 'но́сиш', 'но́сять'
- 'вози́ти': 'вожу́', 'во́зиш', 'во́зять'
- 'леті́ти': 'лечу́', 'лети́ш', 'летя́ть'

The note on spelling and sound explains these changes and the stress.

'Літа́ти' and 'бі́гати' are first conjugation, like 'чита́ти': 'літа́ю', 'літа́єш', 'літа́ють'; 'бі́гаю', 'бі́гаєш', 'бі́гають'.

'Нести́' and 'везти́' are first conjugation with the stress on the ending, like 'іти́': 'несу́', 'несе́ш', 'несе́', 'несемо́', 'несете́', 'несу́ть', and 'везу́', 'везе́ш', 'везу́ть'. 'Бі́гти' has its own present: 'г' becomes 'ж' in every form, and the endings are those of the second conjugation: 'біжу́', 'біжи́ш', 'біжи́ть', 'біжимо́', 'біжите́', 'біжа́ть'.

Most of these verbs build the past in the regular way, by dropping '-ти' and adding '-в', '-ла', '-ли': 'ходи́в', 'ї́здила', 'леті́ли', 'носи́в', 'бі́гали', 'ї́хав'. 'Іти́' builds its past on another stem, as the unit on the past showed: 'ішо́в', 'ішла́', 'ішли́'. Three verbs of one direction have a stem that ends in a consonant, and their masculine past has no '-в', as 'могти́', 'міг' does:

- 'нести́': 'ніс', 'несла́', 'несло́', 'несли́'
- 'везти́': 'віз', 'везла́', 'везло́', 'везли́'
- 'бі́гти': 'біг', 'бі́гла', 'бі́гло', 'бі́гли'

examples.source: I carry my keys in my jacket.
He was carrying the suitcase to the taxi.
Oksana was taking a present to her grandma.
We're flying to Kyiv.
Taras was running for the bus.

grammar.title: Setting off: піти́ and пої́хати
grammar.explanation:
The prefix 'по-' added to a verb of one direction makes a perfective verb that names the start of the movement: setting off. The two most common are 'піти́', from 'іти́', and 'пої́хати', from 'ї́хати'. In 'піти́' the prefix and the verb have merged, but its forms still follow 'іти́': 'піду́' like 'іду́', 'пішо́в' like 'ішо́в'.

The forms:

- 'піти́', future: 'піду́', 'пі́деш', 'пі́де', 'пі́демо', 'пі́дете', 'пі́дуть'
- 'піти́', past: 'пішо́в', 'пішла́', 'пішло́', 'пішли́'
- 'пої́хати', future: 'пої́ду', 'пої́деш', 'пої́де', 'пої́демо', 'пої́дете', 'пої́дуть'
- 'пої́хати', past: 'пої́хав', 'пої́хала', 'пої́хало', 'пої́хали'

Like every perfective verb, these have no present, and their present-looking forms are the future: 'Я піду́ в банк.' (I'll go to the bank). They are the usual way to state a decision or a plan to go somewhere: 'У п’я́тницю ми пої́демо на мо́ре.' (On Friday we'll go to the sea). For a trip fixed for a set time, the present of the verb of one direction is also correct, as the note on choosing the verb showed: 'У п’я́тницю ми ї́демо на мо́ре.'

In the past, 'піти́' and 'пої́хати' say that someone set off; on its own, such a sentence means that the person has left and is not here now. Compare three pasts of one trip to the shop:

- 'Тара́с пішо́в у магази́н.' (Taras has gone to the shop; he is not back)
- 'Тара́с ходи́в у магази́н.' (Taras went to the shop and came back)
- 'Тара́с ішо́в у магази́н.' (Taras was on his way to the shop)

The phrase 'Мені́ тре́ба йти.' (I have to go, literally 'to-me necessary to-go') is what you say when you leave a place.

The unit on the imperative introduced 'ході́мо', the first person plural imperative of 'ходи́ти'. It means 'let's go', on foot and now: 'Ході́мо в кафе́!' (Let's go to the café!)

rows: Taras has gone to the shop.
Taras went to the shop and came back.
Taras was on his way to the shop.
Tomorrow I'll go to the bank.
У п’я́тницю ми пої́демо на мо́ре.
in Friday we will-go to sea
On Friday we'll go to the sea.

When will you go to the post office?
The children have already left for school.

grammar.title: By train, by plane, by taxi: how and where you travel
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian says how you travel in two ways, and both mean the same.

The first is the instrumental with no preposition, as in 'ї́хати авто́бусом' from the unit on the instrumental. The instrumental names the means:

- 'по́їздом': by train
- 'літако́м': by plane
- 'авто́бусом': by bus
- 'метро́': by subway, since 'метро́' never changes

The second is 'на' with the locative, as in 'на авто́бусі' from the unit on directions: 'на по́їзді', 'на літаку́'. 'Літа́к' takes '-у' in the locative, like 'парк', 'у па́рку', because its stem ends in 'к'. 'Таксі́' never changes form, and 'by taxi' is usually 'на таксі́'.

With 'леті́ти' and 'літа́ти' the means is usually left out, because the verb already says it. 'Літако́м' is added when ways of traveling are compared: 'До Оде́си я ї́хала по́їздом, а з Оде́си леті́ла літако́м.' (I went to Odesa by train and flew back from Odesa.)

The goal of a trip is said in three ways:

- a city or a country: 'до' and the genitive, the most common choice ('до Льво́ва', 'до Кана́ди'), or 'у', 'в' and the accusative ('у Львів'). Both are correct.
- a building or a place: 'у', 'в' or 'на' and the accusative, as in the unit on directions ('в аеропо́рт', 'на вокза́л', 'на зупи́нку').
- a person: 'до' and the genitive, for going to see that person: 'Я ї́ду до бабу́сі.' (I'm going to Grandma's)

The starting point takes 'з' and the genitive: 'з Ки́єва', 'з аеропо́рту', 'з вокза́лу'. A place that takes 'на' for the goal takes 'з' for the start: 'на вокза́л', 'з вокза́лу'.

A ticket takes 'до' for the place and 'на' and the accusative for the day or the train: 'квито́к до Льво́ва на п’я́тницю', a ticket to Lviv for Friday; 'квито́к на по́їзд', a train ticket.

rows: Він ї́де до Ки́єва на по́їзді.
he goes to Kyiv on train
He is going to Kyiv by train.
The taxi is coming from the airport.

examples.source: Are you taking the bus to the station?

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: ходжу́, ї́жджу, ношу́, вожу́, лечу́ and по́їзд
grammar.explanation:
Every new word of this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress. The points below are the ones the verbs of motion bring up.

Five verbs change the last consonant of the stem in the 'я' form, and only there:

- 'д' becomes 'дж': 'ходи́ти', 'ходжу́' [xɔˈd͡ʒu]
- 'зд' becomes 'ждж': 'ї́здити', 'ї́жджу' [ˈjiʒd͡ʒu]
- 'с' becomes 'ш': 'носи́ти', 'ношу́' [nɔˈʃu]
- 'з' becomes 'ж': 'вози́ти', 'вожу́' [ʋɔˈʒu]
- 'т' becomes 'ч': 'леті́ти', 'лечу́' [lɛˈt͡ʃu]

The change has a history: long ago the 'я' form of these verbs had a [j] after the consonant, and that [j] turned 'д' into 'дж', 'з' into 'ж', 'с' into 'ш' and 'т' into 'ч'. In 'ї́жджу' both consonants of 'зд' changed: 'з' became 'ж' and 'д' became 'дж'. Remember that 'дж' is one sound, as in 'jam', so 'ї́жджу' has [ʒ] and then [d͡ʒ], with no vowel between them. The other forms keep the plain consonant: 'хо́диш', 'ї́здиш', 'но́сиш', 'во́зиш', 'лети́ш'.

The stress moves in three of these verbs: 'ходжу́', 'ношу́' and 'вожу́' stress the ending, while 'хо́диш', 'но́сиш', 'во́зиш' and the other forms stress the stem. 'Піти́' moves its stress the same way: 'піду́', but 'пі́деш', 'пі́де', 'пі́дуть'. 'Ї́здити' keeps the stress on 'ї' in every form, and 'леті́ти' keeps it on the ending; there the unstressed 'е' of 'лечу́' leans toward 'и'.

'Бі́гти' changes 'г' into 'ж' in every present form: 'біжу́', 'біжи́ш', 'біжа́ть'. In the infinitive the 'г' stands before the voiceless 'т', and here the exception the unit on directions taught with 'ле́гко' and 'могти́' applies: a voiced consonant normally keeps its voice, but 'г' before 'к' or 'т' is said [x], so 'бі́гти' is [ˈbʲixtɪ]. In the past 'біг' it ends the word and stays voiced, [bʲiɦ], because voiced consonants keep their voice at the end of a word.

'Ніс' and 'віз', the masculine pasts of 'нести́' and 'везти́', show the alternation from the unit on nouns: 'е' in an open syllable becomes 'і' in a closed one. The other forms have an open syllable and keep 'е': 'несла́', 'везла́', 'несли́'. 'Ніс', he carried, is spelled and said like the noun 'ніс', nose, and the sentence tells them apart. 'Віз' ends in a voiced [z].

'По́їзд' [ˈpɔjizd] has two syllables. 'Ї' is always [ji], so after 'о' it adds a [j], and the final 'зд' stays voiced. 'Пої́хати' [pɔˈjixɑtɪ] has the same 'ої' with the same [j], because it is 'по-' added to 'ї́хати'.

The other new words:

- 'Аеропо́рт' [ɑɛrɔˈpɔrt] has four syllables; 'а' and 'е' are said one after the other.
- 'Валі́за' has a soft 'л' before 'і'.
- 'Ро́зклад' [ˈrɔzklɑd] keeps the voiced [z] before 'к' and the voiced [d] at the end.
- 'Мі́сце' moves its stress in the plural: 'місця́'.
- 'Літа́к' moves its stress to the ending in the other forms: 'літака́', 'на літаку́'.
- 'По́їзд' keeps its stress on 'о' in the singular and moves it to the ending in the plural: 'поїзди́', 'поїзді́в'.
- 'Таксі́' is stressed on its last syllable and never changes form.

examples.source: I often go to the movies.
I go to Grandma's by train.
I drive Mom to the market.
I'm flying to see my parents.

culture.title: Night trains, tea in a glass and minibuses
culture.text:
For long distances inside Ukraine, most people travel by train. The national railway company is 'Укрзалізни́ця': 'Укр-' is short for Ukrainian, and 'залізни́ця', railway, comes from 'залі́зо', iron, so the word says 'the iron road'. Fast day trains link Kyiv with Lviv, Kharkiv and Dnipro in a few hours, and popular trips lead to Lviv, to Odesa on the Black Sea and to the Carpathian Mountains, 'Карпа́ти', in the west.

The classic Ukrainian journey is the night train: you board in the evening, sleep, and arrive in the morning. Most sleeping cars on a night train are of two kinds:

- 'купе́': a car of closed compartments, each with four beds
- 'плацка́рт': an open car with beds along its whole length, cheaper and more crowded

Every car has its own attendant, 'провідни́к' for a man and 'провідни́ця' for a woman, who checks the tickets at the door, hands out bed linen and sells tea. The tea comes in a glass, 'скля́нка', set in a metal holder, and many travelers say that this tea is part of the trip. A ticket names the car and the seat, so passengers walk along the platform to find their car before they board.

In cities and between small towns, many people travel by minibus, 'маршру́тка', which follows a fixed route and is often faster than a bus.

When someone sets off on a trip, Ukrainians say 'Щасли́вої доро́ги!', Have a good trip!, literally 'of-happy of-road!'. Like 'Смачно́го!', it is a wish in the genitive, with 'бажа́ю', I wish, left out.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian travel words with their English meanings
Match each general verb with its meaning

pairs.source: to go on foot, in general
to go by vehicle, in general

exercises.prompt: Which verb means 'to go by vehicle, in one direction'?
exercises.explanation: 'Ї́хати' is the verb of one direction for any vehicle. 'Іти́' is on foot, and 'ї́здити' is the general verb that pairs with 'ї́хати'.

choices: We are going to Kyiv now.

exercises.prompt: Sam is walking to the station right now. Which word completes 'Сем за́раз ___ на вокза́л.'?
exercises.explanation: The movement is happening now, toward one goal, on foot, so the verb of one direction 'іти́' is used: 'іде́'. 'Хо́дить' would mean that he goes there regularly.

choices: Yesterday we went to the park.
The day before yesterday we went to the park.
The day before yesterday we went to the bank.

exercises.hint_source: I'm carrying the suitcase to the taxi.
exercises.explanation: The suitcase is carried on foot, now, toward one goal, so the verb is 'нести́', and its 'я' form is 'несу́'.

exercises.hint_source: Taras goes to work by bus every day.
exercises.explanation: 'Щодня́' names a habit, and the bus is a vehicle, so the general verb 'ї́здити' is used: 'ї́здить'.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Окса́на ча́сто но́сить цю су́кню.' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'Носи́ти', the general verb of carrying, also means to wear clothes regularly. 'Is carrying' right now would take 'несе́'.

exercises.prompt: Which form is the 'я' form of 'ходи́ти'?
exercises.explanation: In the 'я' form 'д' becomes 'дж', and the stress is on the ending: 'ходжу́'. 'Хо́диш' is the 'ти' form, and 'іду́' belongs to 'іти́'.

exercises.hint_source: I often go to Kyiv by train.
exercises.explanation: A repeated trip by vehicle takes 'ї́здити'. In its 'я' form 'зд' becomes 'ждж': 'ї́жджу'.

choices: We flew to Lviv by plane.
We went to Lviv by train.
We flew to Odesa by plane.

exercises.hint_source: We are flying to Odesa right now.
exercises.explanation: A flight happening now, toward one goal, takes 'леті́ти'. Its 'ми' form is 'летимо́', with the stress on the ending.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Оле́на пішла́ на по́шту.' tell you?
choices: Olena goes to the post office every day.
Olena has gone to the post office and is not back yet.
Olena went to the post office and came back.
exercises.explanation: The past of 'піти́' says that someone set off, and on its own it means that she is not back yet. A trip there and back would be 'Оле́на ходи́ла на по́шту.'

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means the same as 'Учо́ра я був у кіно́.'?
exercises.explanation: The general verb in the past names a trip there and back, so 'ходи́в у кіно́' means that I was at the movies. 'Йшов' says only that I was on my way.

exercises.hint_source: Yesterday Taras walked to the post office and back.
exercises.explanation: A trip on foot there and back in the past takes the general verb 'ходи́ти': 'ходи́в'.

exercises.hint_source: Tomorrow we will go to Lviv.
exercises.explanation: 'Пої́демо', the future of the perfective 'пої́хати', states the plan to set off. The present 'ї́демо' is also correct for a trip fixed for a set time.

exercises.prompt_target: Оле́на вже ___ в аеропо́рт на таксі́.
exercises.hint_source: Olena has already left for the airport by taxi.
exercises.explanation: Someone who has set off by vehicle and is not here now takes the past of 'пої́хати'. Olena is a woman, so the form is 'пої́хала'.

choices: In the 'я' form both consonants of 'зд' change: 'з' to 'ж' and 'д' to 'дж'.
exercises.explanation: Only the 'я' form changes; the others keep 'зд': 'ї́здиш', 'ї́здять'. 'Дж' is one sound, so 'ї́жджу' is said [ˈjiʒd͡ʒu].

exercises.prompt: Why is the past of 'нести́' 'ніс' for a man but 'несла́' for a woman?
choices: 'Е' in an open syllable becomes 'і' in a closed one, and 'ніс' ends in a closed syllable.
'Ніс' is the noun for nose, used as a verb.
The feminine form adds an 'е' that the masculine form lacks.
exercises.explanation: The stem is 'нес-'. In 'ніс' the syllable is closed, so 'е' becomes 'і', as 'о' does in 'кіт', 'кота́'. In 'несла́' the syllable 'не' is open, and the 'е' stays.

exercises.hint_source: Mykola often drives Halyna to the market.
exercises.explanation: Taking someone by vehicle again and again takes the general verb 'вози́ти'. In the 'він' form the 'з' stays and the stress is on the stem: 'во́зить'.
The means of travel is the instrumental: 'по́їздом'. 'По́їзда' is the genitive, and 'до по́їзда' means 'to the train'.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, when does Sam's train to Lviv leave?
exercises.explanation: Bohdan offers trains at seven and at nine, and Sam says 'О сьо́мій, будь ла́ска.' The train at six in the evening is the one back from Lviv on Sunday.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, why does Taras go to the airport every week?
choices: He often flies to Lviv, where his work is.
exercises.explanation: Taras says 'Я ча́сто літа́ю до Льво́ва, бо там моя́ робо́та.' It is Oksana who is flying to see her grandmother.

exercises.prompt: In the third dialogue, how did Olena travel to the Carpathians?
choices: By train to Lviv, then by bus
exercises.explanation: Olena says 'Споча́тку по́їздом до Льво́ва, а по́тім авто́бусом.' It was Sam who flew, to Canada.

exercises.prompt_source: May I have a seat by the window?

exercises.explanation: The past of 'піти́' or 'пої́хати' says that Taras set off and is not here now. 'Пішо́в' is on foot, 'пої́хав' by vehicle.
A flight in progress takes 'леті́ти', and its 'вони́' form is 'летя́ть'. A country takes 'до' and the genitive or 'у' and the accusative.
Nobody walks to Lviv, so the verb is 'пої́хати', and its past says that Sam set off. A city takes 'до' and the genitive or 'у' and the accusative.

exercises.prompt_source: The children are running to school.
exercises.explanation: Running now toward one goal takes 'бі́гти'. Its 'вони́' form is 'біжа́ть', with 'ж' in place of 'г'.

exercises.audio_target: Я ча́сто ї́жджу на робо́ту авто́бусом.
exercises.hint_source: I often go to work by bus.
